messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 72

He is a 49-year-old North American man who comes across as steady and practical at first glance, the kind of person who has spent most of his adult life fixing things that leak, clog, or break under pressure. He has worked as a plumber for years, often taking pride in being the man other people call when something in the house is failing. That sense of usefulness matters to him. It is part of how he has always understood himself. In recent months, though, he has begun to describe his life as feeling narrower, organized around what he can avoid rather than what he can do.

His history of trauma centers on a past romantic relationship that became physically abusive. He describes the early period of that relationship as “normal enough,” with the kind of closeness that made the later violence harder to name at first. The abuse does not begin with a single dramatic incident but unfolds gradually, through shoved shoulders, grabbed arms, objects thrown in anger, and the steady message that he is the one causing the problems. Over time, the relationship becomes a place where he is always bracing, always trying to predict what will set the other person off. He remembers learning to keep his voice flat, to move carefully, to hide fatigue and frustration because any sign of independence could escalate things. He stays longer than he feels he should because he is ashamed, because he tells himself it is temporary, and because he does not know how to explain to others that he is being hurt by someone he loves.

The violence eventually becomes more serious, and he begins to live in a state of constant alertness. He reports that even after leaving the relationship, his body does not seem to understand that the danger is over. Sudden movement startles him. Raised voices make his chest tighten. When someone steps too close behind him, especially in a doorway or a confined space, he feels a surge of heat and the urge to turn quickly, as if he must defend himself before he can think. He notices that he scans rooms automatically, checking exits and watching hands rather than faces. He says he cannot relax in a way that used to feel effortless. Sleep has become a problem; he falls asleep exhausted, then wakes abruptly with his heart racing and a vivid sense that something is wrong. Some nights he lies awake replaying scenes from the relationship, especially the moments when he thinks he should have left sooner or fought back harder. The self-blame is persistent and familiar, woven into how he talks about the abuse, as if his mind keeps returning to the same question of what he could have done differently.

At work, the effects show up in quieter ways. Plumbing requires patience, concentration, and physical confidence, and he still performs the job, but he notices he is less comfortable in cramped basements, behind closed doors, or under sinks where his movement is restricted. He becomes tense when a customer stands over him watching too closely. He sometimes has to stop and take a breath before reaching into dark spaces, though he does not usually explain why. He is proud of being dependable, so he pushes himself to keep going, but the effort leaves him depleted. After a long day, he returns home with the feeling that he has been “holding himself together” since morning. His wife has noticed that he is more distant and jumpy, and he feels guilty that he is harder to live with, though he struggles to talk about what is happening without feeling weak or exposed.

He also carries a deep sense of humiliation about having been hurt by a partner. He has difficulty making sense of how someone he trusted could repeatedly strike him, then apologize, then do it again. That confusion lingers. He is not someone who naturally talks about fear, and he has spent much of his life solving problems through action, not reflection. But he now finds that memory intrudes in ways he cannot control. Certain smells, tones of voice, and the sound of footsteps approaching from behind can pull him back into the atmosphere of the abuse with startling force. He becomes irritable, withdrawn, and easily overwhelmed, then ashamed of those reactions. More than anything, he seems tired of living as if harm is still imminent, as if his body has not received the message that the relationship is over.
